summary.text: The Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain is a mostly underwater line of more than 80 volcanoes stretching about 6,200 km across the Pacific, breaking the surface in Hawaii.

In 1963 John Tuzo Wilson explained it as the work of an essentially stationary hotspot, with the Pacific plate drifting northwest over it and leaving a trail of increasingly eroded islands and seamounts.
The chain bends by about 120°, and researchers still debate whether a change in plate direction or a moving hotspot caused that bend.

facts.value: Many volcanoes honour former emperors of Japan

items.prompt: Picture a sheet of paper sliding slowly over a candle that stays put, leaving a line of scorch marks. If this chain formed that way, where are its oldest volcanoes?

options.label: Right beside the Island of Hawaiʻi
Scattered evenly along the whole chain
At the far northwest end of the chain
In the middle, at the bend

items.explain: The plate drifted northwest over a fixed hotspot, so volcanoes get older toward the northwest; the Emperor seamounts there are the oldest part.

items.prompt: Why does the Island of Hawaiʻi still have active volcanoes when islands far to its northwest do not?

options.label: It has more rainfall to feed the volcanoes
It sits closest to the hotspot
It lies on a different tectonic plate
It was struck by a large meteorite

items.explain: The Hawaiian archipelago is nearest the hotspot, which makes it the youngest and volcanically active part of the chain.

items.prompt: Sailing northwest from Hawaii, volcanic islands give way to atolls and finally to mountains hidden below the waves. What explains this change?

options.label: Older volcanoes went quiet, eroded and sank
Rising sea levels covered only the far islands
Coral reefs grew on top and pushed them down
Earthquakes split the far islands into pieces

items.explain: Farther from the hotspot, erosion overtook volcanic activity, leaving atolls, and the oldest volcanoes subsided below sea level as seamounts.

items.prompt: Rocks from the Emperor seamounts record that the older the seamount, the farther north it first cooled. What does this point to?

options.label: The Pacific plate has never moved
Earth's magnetic field stayed perfectly fixed
The seamounts were dragged south by ocean currents
The hotspot itself has moved over time

items.explain: A fixed hotspot would give the same ancient latitude for every sample; a north-to-south change suggests the hotspot moved in the mantle.

items.prompt: One model blames the chain's bend on a 'trench jam'. What jammed the trench?

options.label: Ice sheets pressing down on the plate
Thick, buoyant seamounts that resisted sinking
A collision with the Hawaiian islands
Lava that hardened inside the trench

items.explain: In Niu's model, the Emperor seamounts reached the northern subduction zone, resisted subduction, and so reoriented the plate's motion.

items.prompt: From near Kamchatka to just off the Island of Hawaiʻi, roughly how long is this chain?

options.label: About 62 km
About 620 km
About 6,200 km
About 62,000 km

items.explain: The chain stretches about 6,200 km (3,900 mi) and holds more than 80 identified undersea volcanoes.

paragraphs.heading: A mountain range under the sea
paragraphs.text: The Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain is a range of mountains in the Pacific Ocean, almost all of it underwater. It breaks the surface only in Hawaii. Along a line running from southeast to northwest, it links islands with seamounts, atolls, shallows, banks and reefs. It holds more than 80 known undersea volcanoes and runs about 6,200 km, from near the Aleutian Trench off Kamchatka to Kamaʻehuakanaloa Seamount, its youngest volcano, just southeast of the Island of Hawaiʻi.

paragraphs.heading: How a hotspot builds a chain
paragraphs.text: In 1963 the geologist John Tuzo Wilson offered an explanation for the chain. He proposed a hotspot, a source of volcanic activity that stayed more or less in one place. The Pacific plate slid northwest over it, so the hotspot left behind a line of volcanic islands and seamounts. The farther along that line, the more worn down they are.

paragraphs.heading: Young islands in the southeast
paragraphs.text: The chain has three parts. The youngest is the Hawaiian archipelago, the islands of the U.S. state of Hawaii, which lie nearest the hotspot and are 400,000 to 5.1 million years old. Four of the five volcanoes on the Island of Hawaiʻi are active, including Kilauea and Mauna Loa, and Maui has one active volcano, Haleakalā. Offshore, Kamaʻehuakanaloa is still growing; it is the only volcano in the chain known to be in the underwater pre-shield stage.

paragraphs.heading: Older islands worn to atolls
paragraphs.text: Next come the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, aged between 7.2 and 27.7 million years. Here erosion won out over volcanic activity long ago, and most of what remains is atolls, atoll islands and extinct islands. Kure Atoll in this group is the most northerly atoll on Earth. A proclamation by Bush made the area part of Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, one of the world's largest protected areas, which limits tourism and called for fishing to end by 2011.

paragraphs.heading: The sunken Emperor seamounts
paragraphs.text: The oldest and most eroded section is the Emperor seamounts, between 39 and 85 million years old. Every volcano here has sunk below the sea to become a seamount or a guyot, and many are named after past emperors of Japan. The line ends at the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench, a subduction zone on Russia's border. Detroit Seamount has the oldest confirmed age, 81 million years, though Meiji Seamount to its north is probably a little older.

paragraphs.heading: The puzzle of the bend
paragraphs.text: The Emperor and Hawaiian sections meet at an angle of about 120°. For a long time this bend was read as a sudden change in the direction the Pacific plate was moving. Later work cast doubt on that. Lava from four seamounts kept a record of the ancient magnetic field, and it shows the latitude where they formed shifting from north to south as the rocks get younger, which suggests the hotspot itself moved through the mantle.

paragraphs.heading: Plate, hotspot, or both
paragraphs.text: Researchers still argue over the cause. In 2004 Yaoling Niu proposed that the bend came mostly from a change in plate motion, plus some hotspot movement. In his model the thick, buoyant Emperor seamounts reached the subduction zone in the north and resisted sinking, a trench jam that turned the plate. Niu also noted that a bend caused purely by the hotspot would need the Pacific plate to stay still from 81 to 43 million years ago, yet magnetic patterns show it moving about 60 mm a year then.
